item.title: Quantum Computing's Security Awakening: 2026 Ushers in the Era of Quantum Defense
item.description: This comprehensive review covers 165 articles published in January 2026, surveying a field undergoing a profound shift. Federal agencies have declared 2026 the “Year of Quantum Security,” the Ethereum Foundation has formed a dedicated post-quantum security team with $2 million in research prizes, and a Jefferies strategist has removed Bitcoin from his model portfolio over quantum threats. Meanwhile, error correction researchers achieve 10,000x reductions in error rates, neutral-atom systems scale toward 100,000-qubit architectures, and the University of Waterloo launches the world’s first open-source full-stack quantum computer. Quantum computing is graduating from laboratory curiosity to infrastructure that must be secured, scaled, and democratized.
item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 165 articles published in January 2026, surveying a field undergoing a profound shift. Federal agencies have declared 2026 the “Year of Quantum Security,” the Ethereum Foundation has formed a dedicated post-quantum security team with $2 million in research prizes, and a Jefferies strategist has removed Bitcoin from his model portfolio over quantum threats. Meanwhile, error correction researchers achieve 10,000x reductions in error rates, neutral-atom systems scale toward 100,000-qubit architectures, and the University of Waterloo launches the world’s first open-source full-stack quantum computer. Quantum computing is graduating from laboratory curiosity to infrastructure that must be secured, scaled, and democratized.

The Security Awakening

2026 has been designated the “Year of Quantum Security” by the FBI and NIST, marking a coordinated shift from theoretical concerns to operational mandates across federal agencies source . A launch event in Washington, D.C. on January 12 brought together federal agencies including the White House, DHS, and CISA to address what officials call the “harvest now, decrypt later” threat—where adversaries steal encrypted data today intending to decrypt it once quantum computers mature source .

The urgency is translating into action. The Ethereum Foundation formed a dedicated Post-Quantum security team and announced the $1 million Poseidon Prize to strengthen the network’s quantum-resistant hash function. Combined with last year’s $1 million Proximity Prize for broader post-quantum research, the foundation has committed $2 million to blockchain defense source . Vitalik Buterin, Ethereum’s co-founder, estimates a 20% probability that quantum computers break current cryptography before 2030.

The financial sector is responding. Christopher Wood, Global Head of Equity Strategy at Jefferies, removed the 10% Bitcoin allocation from his recommended portfolio, replacing it with gold, citing concerns that quantum computing could crack cryptocurrency encryption source . Coinbase formed an Independent Advisory Board on Quantum Computing and Blockchain , bringing in experts including Dan Boneh of Stanford and Scott Aaronson to assess risks source . The board’s first position paper is expected early next year source .

Yet awareness has not translated into preparedness. 56% of mid-sized organizations admit they are not prepared for quantum threats source . Research from Bain & Company finds that 90% of companies lack systems to defend against quantum security threats, while 71% expect attacks within five years source . Only 10% have a roadmap to address quantum risks source .

Bitcoin developers maintain that threats are years away, noting slow progress in quantum computing and ongoing work on post-quantum cryptography source . But the divergence between enterprise anxiety and enterprise preparation is stark. As one analyst put it, companies focused narrowly on AI risk missing the quantum shift source .

The Security Paradox

Even as organizations mobilize against quantum threats to encryption, researchers have exposed a irony: quantum computers themselves have serious security flaws. Researchers at Penn State identified serious security weaknesses in current quantum computing systems, including vulnerabilities in program verification, circuit design, and hardware crosstalk source .

The research, funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and Intel, found that current security methods for classical computers are inadequate for quantum systems source . Swaroop Ghosh, professor of computer science and electrical engineering at Penn State, warns that as quantum computers become more integrated into industry, these flaws could expose sensitive corporate and personal information to theft and tampering source .

The vulnerabilities span multiple layers. Circuit topology issues could enable information encoding tampering, while hardware crosstalk between adjacent qubits could facilitate information leakage source . The researchers argue that protecting quantum computers requires securing both software and physical hardware from the ground up—a multi-layered defense strategy that current systems largely lack source .

This creates a paradox: quantum computing is viewed as an offensive threat to existing encryption, yet quantum systems themselves are vulnerable to attack. As industry adoption grows, addressing these foundational security challenges will be essential before quantum computers can be safely deployed for sensitive commercial and research applications source .

Error Correction Breakthroughs

The technical community is actively addressing quantum computing’s central challenge: error correction. Several advances this month demonstrate real progress toward fault-tolerant systems.

Cat Qubit Advances

Alice & Bob announced “Elevator Codes” , a new approach to error correction for cat qubit quantum computers source . The technique uses code concatenation to achieve a 10,000 times lower logical error rate compared to current error correction methods, requiring only 3 times more qubits source .

Diego Ruiz, theoretical physicist at Alice & Bob, notes that this reduction could enable complex molecular simulations sooner than expected source . The company, which has raised €130 million and hired 150 employees, claims its approach reduces hardware requirements for a large-scale quantum computer by 200 times source .

AI-Assisted Decoding

EdenCode emerged from stealth with $1.3 million in pre-seed funding to develop a real-time AI decoder for quantum error correction source . The San Jose-based startup, founded by Dr. Wanda Hou (CEO) and Prof. Yi-Zhuang You of UC San Diego, claims its hardware-agnostic neural network achieves a 99.9% error-detection rate and operates up to 10 times faster than conventional methods source .

The technology aims to reduce error rates by a factor of 10 and processes faults in less than a millisecond source . This addresses a critical bottleneck: as quantum systems scale, decoding delays can increase, but EdenCode’s approach is designed to scale without increasing processing time source .

Research & Tools

The snaQCs2025 project, a German consortium including neQxt GmbH, Fraunhofer Institute for Applied Solid State Physics IAF, and Point 8 GmbH, launched with €2.5 million in government funding to advance quantum error correction with logical qubits source . The three-year project aims to create a complete development pipeline from simulation to hardware integration source .

Nature published a demonstration of low-overhead quantum error correction codes, representing peer-reviewed validation of progress in the field source .

Microsoft released an updated, open-source Quantum Development Kit focused on creating fault-tolerant quantum applications source . The release includes specialized toolkits for chemistry and error correction, with the full error correction suite expected by late 2026 source . The kit integrates Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot to simplify quantum programming source .

Scaling Up: Hardware Advances

Neutral-Atom Scaling

Neutral-atom quantum computing emerged as a leading platform for scaling this month. Researchers at Columbia University demonstrated a new method combining optical tweezers with metasurfaces, successfully trapping 1,000 strontium atoms and creating a metasurface capable of generating 360,000 optical tweezers source . This lays groundwork for quantum computers with over 100,000 qubits source .

The approach overcomes bulk and cost limitations of previous technologies like spatial light modulators source . For comparison, a Caltech team achieved 6,100 trapped atoms using previous methods source . The Columbia team’s metasurface uses 200 nm pixels—smaller than the wavelength of light—and tolerates optical intensities up to 2,000 W/mm² source . The research was published in Nature source .

Moscow State University and Rosatom successfully tested a 72-qubit neutral-atom quantum computer prototype , utilizing rubidium atoms in optical tweezers with a novel three-zone architecture source . The system achieved 94% two-qubit gate accuracy, fulfilling a 2024 government mandate to scale neutral-atom platforms beyond 50 qubits source . Russia is targeting fault-tolerant quantum systems by 2030 source .

Silicon Progress

Researchers in Australia demonstrated an 11-qubit quantum processor using phosphorus atoms in isotopically-pure silicon-28, achieving gate fidelities above 99% source . The system operates at 16 mK and successfully created entangled states of up to eight atoms without performance degradation as qubits were added source .

This silicon-based approach shows promise for easier scaling than superconducting or ion-trap qubits, as it leverages existing semiconductor manufacturing expertise source . The work was published in Nature in 2025 source .

Commercial Deployments

Rigetti Computing received an $8.4 million order to deliver a 108-qubit quantum computer to India’s Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC) source . The system, featuring Rigetti’s chiplet-based architecture, is scheduled for on-premises deployment in Bengaluru in the second half of 2026 source . This builds on a memorandum of understanding signed in September 2025 focused on hybrid quantum-classical computing systems source .

Rigetti’s superconducting systems operate with gate speeds of 50-70ns, which the company notes is approximately 1,000 times faster than ion traps and neutral atoms source . The company has previously sold systems with up to 180 qubits source .

The deployment is part of India’s broader quantum initiatives. The country’s National Quantum Mission has a budget of approximately $730 million source . Domestic developments include QpiAI’s 25-qubit Indus system, with a 64-qubit Kaveri processor planned source .

Capital Flows to Quantum

Equal1, an Irish quantum semiconductor company, raised $60 million (€51 million) in a funding round led by the Ireland Strategic Investment Fund source . The company’s Bell-1 QPU uses silicon spin qubits built on standard silicon, enabling integration with existing data centers source . The funds will support deployment in European HPC centers and acceleration of the roadmap toward millions of on-chip qubits source . A key deployment is planned for the European Space Agency’s High Performance Compute Centre source . Equal1’s CMOS-manufactured hybrid quantum-classical silicon-on-chip (QSoC) architecture aims to reduce cost and infrastructure barriers source .

Photonic, a Canadian quantum computing company, secured $130 million ($180M CAD) in funding led by Planet First Partners, bringing total capital raised to $271 million ($375M CAD) source . The company is developing fault-tolerant systems combining silicon-based qubits with photonic connectivity using its “Entanglement First Architecture” source . The funding will advance product milestones, expand teams, and deepen customer engagements source .

Microsoft launched the 2026 Quantum Research Pioneers Program (QuPP) , inviting academic researchers to submit proposals for funding up to $200,000 to advance measurement-based approaches for topological quantum computing source . The program focuses on challenges including simulation methods, error correction, and control techniques, with funding decisions announced March 15 and the program beginning August 1, 2026 source .

Democratizing Quantum Access

The University of Waterloo launched Open Quantum Design (OQD) , the world’s first open-source, full-stack quantum computer using ion-trapping technology source . OQD provides open access to quantum hardware and software, partnering with Haiqu, Unitary Foundation, and Xanadu to accelerate quantum computing development source . The initiative has 30 software contributors and builds on 8 years of hardware development at the Institute for Quantum Computing (IQC) source .

Co-founders Crystal Senko, Rajibul Islam, and Roger Melko aim to promote collaboration by providing real hardware access for algorithm testing source . This open-source model could accelerate quantum computing development by enabling broader collaboration source .

Sri Lanka inaugurated its first quantum computer , a nuclear magnetic resonance-powered system from Spinqiu housed at the University of Colombo source . The facility will enable hands-on learning and advanced research in quantum mechanics, positioning the country on the global quantum innovation map source .

Colorado School of Mines launched the first undergraduate Bachelor of Science in Quantum Systems Engineering in the United States source . The program addresses the quantum workforce gap through an interdisciplinary curriculum and industry collaboration, including a year-long, industry-sponsored capstone project and access to the Quantum Commons hub source . The first students will enroll Fall 2026, with inaugural graduates expected Spring 2029 source . The program is supported by the Elevate Quantum consortium, which includes 120 organizations source .

The Enterprise Readiness Gap

An IBM study of 2,000 executives across 33 countries and 23 industries reveals a striking disconnect: 59% believe quantum-enabled AI will transform their industry by 2030, but only 27% expect their organizations to be using quantum computing by then source . This 32-percentage-point gap indicates significant underpreparation source .

The study finds that 79% of respondents say AI will significantly contribute to revenue by 2030, but companies focused narrowly on AI risk missing the quantum shift source . Quantum computing will integrate with classical computing as complementary tools in hybrid workflows source .

Early adopters are already experimenting. Moderna uses 80-qubit systems to model mRNA secondary structures, while larger optimization problems use 156-qubit systems with 950 non-local gates source . HSBC is exploring quantum for financial optimization source .

The quantum computing market is projected to reach $72 billion by 2035 (high-end projection) or $28 billion (low-end) source . McKinsey estimates quantum computing could unlock $100 billion in value by 2035 source .

Quandela, a photonic quantum computing company, identified four key trends for 2026 : hybrid quantum-classical computing, industrial use cases, error correction, and cybersecurity source . These trends indicate quantum computing is moving from research laboratories to practical adoption source . In Canada, the quantum sector is projected to contribute $17.7 billion to GDP and generate 157,000 jobs by 2045 source .

Global Quantum Alliances

International partnerships accelerated this month. Singapore and Japan signed a Memorandum of Cooperation on quantum technology, establishing a bilateral framework with 8 priority areas source . Concurrently, Japanese hardware startup Yaqumo Inc. and Singapore-based Entropica Labs signed an MOU to collaborate on hardware-software co-design for fault-tolerant quantum computers using cold-atom systems source .

The European Photonics for Quantum (P4Q) pilot will launch in 2026 with €50 million in funding, involving 29 partners across 12 countries source . The project focuses on silicon nitride and thin-film lithium niobate photonic chips, aiming to improve reliability and scalability for quantum applications source .

PsiQuantum and Airbus announced a partnership to develop fault-tolerant quantum algorithms for aerospace applications, focusing on computational fluid dynamics source . They co-authored a technical paper presenting a Quantum Lattice Boltzmann Algorithm validated for aircraft aerodynamics, utilizing PsiQuantum’s Construct software suite source .

Quobly and TNO partnered to optimize silicon spin qubit manufacturing , focusing on bridging device engineering and materials science to improve yield and performance source .

Horizon Quantum Computing and Alice & Bob announced a strategic collaboration to accelerate fault-tolerant quantum computing software development source . The partnership integrates Alice & Bob’s quantum emulators with Horizon’s Triple Alpha development platform source .

IQM Quantum Computers and Bechtle will install a five-qubit Spark quantum computer at Heilbronn University of Applied Sciences in Germany later this year source . Bechtle will provide operational support and maintenance for the first three years source .

Ohio Representative Heidi Workman introduced House Bill 650 to establish the Frontier Technologies and Quantum Computing Commission source . The bipartisan commission will study emerging technologies including AI, quantum computing, and biotechnology to inform policy and position Ohio as a leader in innovation source .

The European Quantum Act, set for adoption in 2026, aims to align investment, governance, security, and deployment of quantum technologies to strengthen Europe’s sovereignty and competitiveness source . The policy initiative seeks to bridge gaps in patents and private capital while integrating cryptographic protections like post-quantum cryptography source .

Looking Ahead

The developments of January 2026 reveal quantum computing at a crossroads. The security awakening—marked by the “Year of Quantum Security” designation, Ethereum’s urgent response, and growing investor anxiety—signals that quantum is being taken seriously as infrastructure source . The technical advances in error correction (Alice & Bob’s 10,000x improvement, EdenCode’s real-time AI decoding) and hardware scaling (Columbia’s 360,000 optical tweezers, Russia’s 72-qubit prototype) show the field is solving real engineering challenges source .

The funding momentum (Equal1’s $60M, Photonic’s $130M) reflects investor confidence in specific technical approaches, particularly silicon-based systems compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing source . The open-source initiative (Open Quantum Design) and workforce development efforts (Colorado School of Mines degree) address the democratization and talent pipeline challenges source .

But the IBM study reveals a persistent enterprise readiness gap: 59% expect quantum AI to transform industries by 2030, but only 27% are preparing to use it source . Only 10% of companies have a roadmap to address quantum risks, despite 71% expecting attacks within five years source .

The pattern is clear: quantum computing is maturing from science project to infrastructure, but adoption will lag behind capability. 2026 is about preparing for a quantum future that’s still years away, but no longer theoretical. As Quandela’s trends indicate, the focus has shifted to hybrid quantum-classical computing, industrial use cases, error correction, and cybersecurity source . The question is no longer whether quantum computing will arrive, but whether organizations will be ready when it does.

item.title: April 2025: Error Correction Breakthroughs, New Benchmarks, and the Path to Quantum Utility
item.description:
This comprehensive review covers 185 articles published in April 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing. This month brought remarkable progress in quantum reliability: Alice & Bob demonstrated cat qubits with 160x fewer errors , while researchers unveiled the first comprehensive benchmark showing quantum systems surpassing classical simulation limits. Beyond the lab, governments committed hundreds of millions, and new quantum systems came online worldwide.

Reliability Breakthrough: Cat Qubits Get 160x Better

The most significant technical advance this month came from Alice & Bob, which achieved a 160x reduction in bit-flip errors using “squeezed” cat qubits. The technique extends cat qubit lifetime from 138 milliseconds to 22 seconds—a dramatic improvement that makes error correction considerably less resource-intensive. Bit-flip errors, where a qubit spontaneously flips from \(|0\rangle\) to \(|1\rangle\), are one of the two fundamental error types in quantum computing. Suppressing them at the hardware level reduces the overhead required for software-based error correction.
item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 185 articles published in April 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing. This month brought remarkable progress in quantum reliability: Alice & Bob demonstrated cat qubits with 160x fewer errors , while researchers unveiled the first comprehensive benchmark showing quantum systems surpassing classical simulation limits. Beyond the lab, governments committed hundreds of millions, and new quantum systems came online worldwide.

Reliability Breakthrough: Cat Qubits Get 160x Better

The most significant technical advance this month came from Alice & Bob, which achieved a 160x reduction in bit-flip errors using “squeezed” cat qubits. The technique extends cat qubit lifetime from 138 milliseconds to 22 seconds—a dramatic improvement that makes error correction considerably less resource-intensive. Bit-flip errors, where a qubit spontaneously flips from \(|0\rangle\) to \(|1\rangle\), are one of the two fundamental error types in quantum computing. Suppressing them at the hardware level reduces the overhead required for software-based error correction.

The squeezing technique works without modifying circuit design, making it potentially applicable to existing cat qubit architectures. Cat qubits are a type of bosonic code that encodes quantum information in the oscillations of a superconducting resonator, named after Schrodinger’s famous thought experiment. By squeezing the quantum state, the researchers effectively narrowed the uncertainty in one quadrature while expanding it in the orthogonal direction—trading one type of error for another that’s easier to correct.

Complementary Error Correction Advances

Alice & Bob’s breakthrough is part of a broader set of error correction advances this month:

  • University of Twente researchers invented a photonic error correction method that filters high-quality photons at the source rather than correcting errors after the fact. Previous approaches required hundreds of physical photons to create a single reliable logical qubit; the new technique dramatically reduces this overhead, making photonic quantum computers cheaper and more practical.

  • Scientists at the University of Witwatersrand developed optical skyrmions —topological structures formed in entangled photon pairs that encode quantum information in their global properties rather than local states. Even when entanglement degrades, the topological protection helps preserve information, potentially enabling more robust quantum networks.

  • Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory researchers reduced superinductor capacitance by over 60% through a new chemical etching process that suspends superinductors above the wafer surface. This cuts substrate-related noise, a major source of error in superconducting qubits, and provides a practical fabrication method for scaling up.

  • UCL engineers broke a 25-year barrier in chip fabrication by using arsenic atoms instead of phosphorus for single-atom placement. They achieved 97% accuracy in positioning individual atoms—compared to the 70% success rate typical for phosphorus—demonstrating a path toward near-zero failure rates in quantum chip manufacturing.

These advances represent complementary approaches to the same fundamental challenge: making quantum computations reliable enough to be useful. While each targets different qubit modalities—superconducting, photonic, topological, silicon-based—together they indicate rapid progress across the field.

Measuring Progress: When Do Quantum Computers Win?

A critical development this month came from the Jülich Research Centre, which unveiled a comprehensive benchmark comparing 19 quantum processing units from five suppliers (IBM, Quantinuum, IonQ, Rigetti, and IQM). Built around the MaxCut optimization problem, the benchmark provides a platform-agnostic way to measure quantum performance as systems scale.

The results revealed important differences between platforms. Quantinuum’s H2-1 passed the benchmark at 56 qubits—a scale that surpasses exact classical simulation. The test used 4,620 two-qubit gates in a Linear Ramp Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (LR-QAOA) circuit, demonstrating that trapped-ion systems can maintain coherence at useful scales.

IBM’s processors showed different strengths: the Fez chip handled 100-qubit problems at depths up to 10,000 layers, though coherent information was retained only through approximately 300 layers. More importantly, the newer Marrakesh chip demonstrated half the error rate per layered gate compared to Fez, showing rapid iterative improvement in IBM’s superconducting hardware.

Benchmarking Software Performance

Separately, researchers introduced Benchpress, an open-source benchmarking suite for quantum software development kits. The suite includes 1,066 tests covering circuit construction, manipulation, and compilation across SDKs including Qiskit, Cirq, Braket, Tket, and others. In initial tests, Qiskit completed circuit construction tests in 2.0 seconds while Tket required 14.2 seconds—but Tket produced circuits with fewer two-qubit gates for certain decompositions, highlighting different performance tradeoffs.

The Challenge of Meaningful Benchmarks

The quest for meaningful benchmarks also revealed ongoing controversies. IEEE Spectrum published a critique of D-Wave’s quantum supremacy claims , noting that the company’s annealing approach solves different problems than gate-based quantum computers and that direct comparisons are often misleading. New Scientist similarly examined why quantum computers continue to fail certain key tests, emphasizing that cross-entropy benchmarking—while useful for measuring random circuit sampling—may not capture performance on practical applications.

This tension between demonstrating raw quantum advantage and solving useful problems remains central to the field. The MaxCut benchmark represents progress because it’s based on a real optimization problem with commercial applications, rather than an artificial benchmark designed solely to showcase quantum speedups.

Building the Quantum Internet: QNodeOS and Distributed Computing

Quantum Operating System

Researchers unveiled QNodeOS, billed as the world’s first operating system for quantum computers . The system enables multiple quantum computers to be controlled centrally and connected for distributed quantum computing—a foundational capability for a future quantum internet. QNodeOS handles resource allocation, job scheduling, and network management across diverse quantum hardware, abstracting away the differences between systems from different vendors.

Network Infrastructure

The UK demonstrated a 410-kilometer quantum network integrating both quantum key distribution (QKD) and entanglement distribution . The network connects multiple nodes and represents a step toward practical quantum communication infrastructure. Simultaneously, the UK launched its Integrated Quantum Networks Hub at Heriot-Watt University, bringing together academia and industry to pioneer secure quantum networks .

In the United States, IonQ and the Electric Power Board (EPB) launched a $22 million Quantum Innovation Center in Chattanooga, Tennessee. The center will house IonQ quantum computing systems and establish the first U.S. hub dedicated to quantum computing and networking research.

New Deployments

IQM announced it will install Poland’s first superconducting quantum computer at Wroclaw University of Science and Technology. The system will support Polish research in quantum algorithms and materials science.

Hardware Milestones: New Systems Come Online

Japan

Fujitsu and RIKEN unveiled a 256-qubit superconducting quantum computer , quadrupling the qubit count of their previous 64-qubit system. The new system builds on Fujitsu’s ongoing collaboration with RIKEN and represents a significant step toward Japan’s goal of developing a domestically produced quantum computing stack.

Separately, ULVAC delivered a cryogenic system for Japan’s first fully domestic quantum computer , supporting the country’s push for end-to-end sovereign quantum capabilities.

India

QpiAI launched the QpiAI-Indus, India’s first full-stack 25-qubit quantum computer under the country’s National Quantum Mission. The system features superconducting qubits and includes both cloud access and on-premises deployment options. India’s quantum push has gained momentum following a government commitment of approximately $1 billion over five years.

Europe

Beyond the IQM deployment in Poland, several European quantum initiatives advanced this month. The UK’s quantum hubs continued their work on networking and applications, while Norway announced new investment in quantum technology research .

Mobile Systems

SaxonQ demonstrated applications running on a mobile quantum computer powered by Quantum Machines’ control electronics. The demonstration showed that room-temperature quantum computing—using nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond—can operate outside specialized data center environments, opening possibilities for field-deployed quantum sensors and computers.

Company/Organization Qubits Technology Location Status
Fujitsu-RIKEN 256 Superconducting Japan Operational
QpiAI 25 Superconducting India Launched
IQM Not specified Superconducting Poland (WUST) Announced
SaxonQ Not specified NV Center (room temp) Mobile Demonstrated

Research Highlights: From Quasiparticles to Topology

Mathematical Applications

Researchers used Quantinuum’s H2-2 quantum computer to explore knot theory , demonstrating how quantum systems can solve complex mathematical problems. The work involved implementing quantum algorithms to compute knot invariants—mathematical quantities that distinguish different types of knots—with potential applications in topological quantum computing and quantum field theory.

In a separate study, researchers demonstrated quantum computing for contingency analysis in power systems , showing how quantum algorithms could identify potentially dangerous configurations in electrical grids more efficiently than classical methods.

Physics Discoveries

National Science Foundation-funded researchers discovered a new quantum quasiparticle : fractional excitons, which carry fractions of an electron’s charge and could enable new approaches to quantum information storage and manipulation.

Researchers observed a superradiant phase transition that had been predicted for 50 years but never seen until now. The phenomenon, observed in a trapped-ion quantum simulator, could advance our understanding of open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.

Quantinuum’s H2 system was used to simulate quantum magnetism using digital quantum simulation techniques, providing insights into magnetic materials that are difficult to study classically.

Hardware Advances

Trapped ion systems achieved a milestone in mid-circuit measurement and reset , capabilities essential for error correction and algorithm efficiency. The ability to measure qubits mid-computation without disturbing neighboring qubits, then reset and reuse them, dramatically reduces the qubit overhead required for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Practical Applications

Google Quantum AI published research on practical applications of its quantum computers , emphasizing work toward quantum advantage in materials simulation and optimization problems.

Researchers demonstrated quantum machine learning for predicting proton affinity , achieving superior accuracy compared to classical methods. Proton affinity is a key property in chemistry and drug discovery, with applications ranging from catalyst design to understanding biochemical reactions.

In China, researchers demonstrated quantum-assisted fine-tuning of billion-parameter AI models , illustrating the convergence of quantum computing and artificial intelligence—a trend that accelerated throughout 2025.

Government Bets: DARPA, UK, and Global Investment

DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative

The U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) made significant moves in quantum computing this month. The agency’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI) selected 18 companies for Stage A awards of approximately $1 million each. The winners include:

  • Atom Computing — Selected for neutral atom quantum computing exploration
  • IonQ — Selected to advance utility-scale quantum computing

The program targets utility-scale quantum systems by 2033 , with DARPA taking an agnostic approach to qubit modalities. Stage A requires companies to develop conceptual descriptions of how they would achieve a logical qubit error rate of \(10^{-6}\) or better—a threshold considered necessary for practical quantum advantage.

UK Quantum Investment

The UK government announced £121 million in funding for quantum applications in fraud detection, anti-money laundering, and cybersecurity . The investment targets practical applications where quantum computing could provide near-term value, though some analysts questioned whether the amount is sufficient given the scale of the challenge.

Other Government Initiatives

  • Norway announced new investment in quantum technology research , strengthening its national quantum capabilities.
  • Colorado received a $40.5 million federal grant for quantum technology development, solidifying the state’s position as a U.S. quantum hub.
  • Italy finalized its national quantum strategy , positioning the country to compete in the European quantum ecosystem.
  • The EU explored quantum computing applications in the energy sector, examining how quantum algorithms could optimize power grids .
  • National security concerns gained prominence, with analyses of quantum threats to nuclear command and control systems and the UK’s quantum security posture .

USA (DARPA) ~$18M (Stage A) Utility-scale systems, benchmarking Target: 2033
UK £121M Fraud detection, AML, cybersecurity Immediate deployment

Italy Not specified National quantum strategy Strategic framework

Industry and Partnerships: Quantum Goes Commercial

Healthcare & Research Partnerships

CAS (a division of the American Chemical Society) and Cleveland Clinic formed a strategic collaboration to advance brain health research using AI and quantum computing. The partnership aims to shorten the typical 17-year timeline from lab discovery to approved therapy, with initial projects focusing on Alzheimer’s drug discovery.

The Milner Therapeutics Institute at Cambridge University signed an MOU with Yonsei University to foster joint quantum computing research. Yonsei will utilize Korea’s first IBM Quantum Computer for collaborative projects, aiming to synergize quantum computing with AI-driven drug discovery.

Investments & Funding

  • BTQ Technologies signed a term sheet to invest €2 million in QPerfect , a neutral atom quantum computing company. The investment grants BTQ a 16.67% equity stake with an option for full ownership within 12 months. QPerfect’s MIMIQ platform provides quantum design automation and simulation capabilities.

  • Rigetti Computing closed a $35 million strategic investment from Quanta Computer, finalizing the investment portion of their collaboration agreement. The partnership aims to combine Quanta’s manufacturing expertise with Rigetti’s superconducting quantum technology.

  • IQM, the Finnish quantum startup, is seeking approximately €128 million in a new funding round as the quantum computing industry sees increased investor interest.

  • IBM announced plans to spend approximately $150 billion on quantum computing over the coming decade, though analysts questioned whether the full amount represents direct quantum investment or broader computational infrastructure.

Technology Partnerships

  • Quantum Machines partnered with NVIDIA’s Accelerated Quantum Research Center to integrate quantum processors with AI supercomputers . The collaboration will use NVIDIA’s GB200 Grace Blackwell Superchips and QM’s OPX1000 control system to enhance quantum-classical communication.

  • Fujitsu expanded its quantum collaboration with RIKEN following the unveiling of their 256-qubit system, strengthening Japan’s domestic quantum capabilities.

  • Terra Quantum announced a strategic partnership with Siemens , targeting quantum applications in industrial optimization and sensing.

  • IonQ expanded its quantum collaboration in Japan through a memorandum of understanding with AIST (National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology), strengthening the company’s presence in the Asian market.

Government Contracts

  • Quantum Computing Inc. (QCi) was awarded a contract to support NASA’s space-based lidar data analysis , applying quantum algorithms to Earth observation data.

  • A UK consortium received a £4.7 million award targeting fault-tolerant quantum computing , accelerating research toward error-corrected quantum systems.

Industry Trends: Market Growth, AI Convergence, and Realistic Expectations

Market Projections

The quantum computing market is projected to reach $2.2 billion by 2027 , according to industry surveys. This growth is driven by increasing enterprise adoption, government investment, and maturing hardware platforms.

Survey data indicates that 83% of quantum professionals expect quantum utility to arrive within a decade , reflecting growing confidence in the field’s trajectory. However, expectations vary significantly by sector and application area.

Quantum-AI Convergence

The convergence of quantum computing and artificial intelligence accelerated this month. Observers noted that quantum SDKs are evolving into Quantum AI SDKs , reflecting the growing integration of quantum computing with machine learning workflows. Google in particular is exploring how quantum computing could supercharge its AI ambitions , potentially using quantum systems for training optimization or inference acceleration.

Geographic Competition

The race for quantum advantage has distinct geographic dimensions. Chicago is positioning itself as a quantum hub with $500 million in state investment , leveraging its concentration of quantum research institutions and companies. Meanwhile, the U.S.-China competition in quantum technology continues to shape national strategies and investment priorities.

Sector-Specific Applications

Industry analyses explored quantum computing’s potential across sectors:

  • Finance: Quantum computing could deliver $450-850 billion in value by 2035 , according to market projections, with applications in portfolio optimization, risk analysis, and fraud detection.

  • Supply Chains: Quantum algorithms may improve supply chain optimization by solving complex logistics problems more efficiently than classical methods.

  • Cryptography: The impact of quantum computing on cryptography continues to drive urgency around post-quantum cryptography migration.

Realistic Expectations

Nature published a cautionary perspective on quantum hype , reminding readers that progress is incremental and that many announced “breakthroughs” represent engineering milestones rather than revolutionary leaps. The article emphasized the gap between qubit counts and useful quantum advantage, noting that error correction remains the fundamental challenge.

Similarly, CNBC questioned whether Google and IBM’s bullish quantum optimism is justified , given that practical quantum advantage remains unproven for most commercial applications. The article noted that while technical progress is real, timelines for commercial viability may be longer than company PR suggests.

World Quantum Day 2025 (April 14) provided an occasion for industry reflection, with various stakeholders weighing in on the state of quantum computing . The consensus view acknowledged significant technical progress while emphasizing that the field remains in early stages.

Looking Ahead: What April 2025 Tells Us

The developments of April 2025 reveal a field making measurable, incremental progress on multiple fronts. Error correction advances—Alice & Bob’s cat qubits, photonic distillation, superinductor improvements, atomically precise fabrication—are systematically reducing the error rates that have long limited quantum computations. New benchmarks like MaxCut and Benchpress are giving us better ways to measure that progress and compare different approaches objectively.

Hardware deployments are expanding both in scale and geography. Japan’s 256-qubit system, India’s first full-stack quantum computer, and Poland’s inaugural superconducting system demonstrate that quantum computing is becoming a global endeavor. Governments are placing serious bets: DARPA’s 2033 target for utility-scale systems, the UK’s application-focused £121 million investment, and various national strategies all signal institutional commitment to quantum advantage.

The convergence with AI is accelerating, though it remains unclear whether quantum systems will provide meaningful advantages for machine learning in the near term. The finance sector continues to lead in commercial experimentation, while healthcare partnerships like CAS-Cleveland Clinic suggest quantum computing may find early applications in drug discovery and molecular simulation.

Yet challenges remain. Nature’s critique of quantum hype serves as a useful reminder that technical milestones don’t automatically translate to commercial advantage. The gap between laboratory demonstrations and reliable, scalable quantum systems is still substantial. Error correction, while improving, remains resource-intensive. And meaningful benchmarks that measure practical advantage—rather than contrived problems—are only beginning to emerge.

The pattern is clear: progress is happening, but it’s engineering-focused and cumulative rather than sudden and revolutionary. DARPA’s 2033 target for utility-scale quantum computing seems increasingly plausible given the rate of improvement in error rates and system scale. But the question remains which approach—superconducting, trapped ion, neutral atom, photonic—will reach practical utility first.

April 2025 didn’t deliver a single “breakthrough” that changed everything. Instead, it delivered something more valuable: evidence that multiple quantum computing approaches are making steady progress on the fundamental challenges that have limited the field for years. That may be less exciting than headlines promise, but it’s the reality of quantum computing in 2025—and it’s enough to keep the field moving forward.

item.content:encoded:
When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang declared practical quantum computing decades away at CES 2025, quantum stocks tanked. Yet January saw record-breaking technical achievements, over $300 million in venture funding, and major product launches. The disconnect between market skepticism and technical progress has never been clearer.

This comprehensive review covers 95 articles published during January 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing.

The Market Shock Heard ‘Round Quantum

On January 8, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CES attendees that practical quantum computing is 15-30 years away , arguing that current qubits need 5-6 orders of magnitude improvement. The next day, quantum computing stocks plummeted. D-Wave dropped 36%, while IonQ, Rigetti Computing, and Quantum Computing Inc. each fell 40-50%—wiping out over $8 billion in combined market value.

Industry leaders forcefully pushed back. D-Wave CEO Dr. Alan Baratz called Huang’s assessment an “egregious error ” and cited a real customer example: a telecommunications optimization problem that took 25 hours on classical computers but just 40 seconds on D-Wave’s quantum annealer. IonQ CEO Peter Chapman disputed the timeline, citing current applications and forecasting $1 billion in revenue by 2030.

The irony: days after downplaying quantum’s prospects, Nvidia announced its first-ever Quantum Day at GTC 2025. The company also promoted 2025 as “the year to become quantum ready .”

Stakeholder Position Key Argument
Jensen Huang (Nvidia CEO) Skeptic Practical quantum computing is 15-30 years away; qubits need 5-6 orders of magnitude improvement
Alan Baratz (D-Wave CEO) Defender Called claim “egregious error”; cited customer case: 25 hours to 40 seconds optimization
Peter Chapman (IonQ CEO) Defender Disputed timeline; cited current quantum applications and $1B revenue forecast by 2030
Mark Luo (Quantum Brilliance CEO) Defender Challenged timeline; highlighted room-temperature diamond qubits delivering value today
Mark Zuckerberg (Meta CEO) Skeptic Echoed Huang’s skepticism, triggered second stock drop later in January

What Actually Happened: Technical Progress in January

While markets gyrated, researchers delivered measurable advances. The headline: MIT achieved a 99.998% single-qubit gate fidelity using fluxonium superconducting qubits—the highest recorded for superconducting technology. The team developed new control techniques including commensurate pulses and circularly polarized microwave drives to address counter-rotating errors that limit fast gates.

Fidelity Records

MIT’s achievement builds on prior work demonstrating 99.92% two-qubit gate fidelity . The advance reduces computational overhead for quantum error correction, bringing fault-tolerant quantum computing closer to reality. Five separate publications covered this milestone, reflecting its significance in the field.

The fluxonium approach uses a superinductor circuit element that creates a more complex energy structure than traditional transmon qubits, enabling higher-fidelity operations. The MIT team’s methods are “platform-independent,” meaning they could be applied to other superconducting qubit architectures.

New Qubit Frontiers

Researchers expanded beyond traditional qubit types:

  • Durham University achieved long-lasting quantum entanglement between molecules using “magic-wavelength optical tweezers,” with entanglement fidelity exceeding 92% and coherence lasting nearly a second . This world-first demonstrates precise control of individual molecules for quantum applications.

  • Harvard scientists trapped ultra-cold polar molecules to perform quantum operations for the first time, entangling two sodium-cesium molecules with 94% accuracy to form a key quantum logic gate. After 20 years of effort, this is considered the final building block needed for molecular quantum computers.

  • UNSW engineers created a “Schrödinger’s cat” state using an antimony atom embedded in a silicon chip. The atom’s eight spin directions allow it to withstand up to seven consecutive errors before data corruption, offering inherent resilience for quantum error correction.

Error Correction Advances

Multiple paths to fault tolerance emerged in January:

  • LDPC-cat codes: Researchers combined low-density parity check codes with cat qubits to create a low-overhead architecture requiring only 758 cat qubits to implement 100 logical qubits—dramatically fewer than traditional approaches.

  • Code-switching: European researchers demonstrated the first error-solving using dual correction codes on an ion-trap quantum computer, enabling fault-tolerant universal computing by switching between 7-qubit color codes and 10-qubit codes.

  • Zero-noise extrapolation: A team led by Zhejiang University integrated ZNE error mitigation with quantum error correction on 13-qubit repetition code circuits , successfully reducing residual errors even as circuit complexity increased.

  • Distributed error correction: Nu Quantum released theory on distributed quantum error correction using modular architectures with hyperbolic Floquet codes, showing fault-tolerant machines are feasible with realistic network and processor fidelities (99.5% entanglement fidelity for interconnects, 99.99% local gate fidelity ).

Hardware Breakthroughs

Chalmers University of Technology and the University of Maryland developed an autonomous quantum refrigerator that cools superconducting qubits to a record-low 22 millikelvin —significantly below the 50 millikelvin achieved by current dilution refrigerators. This increases the qubit’s probability of being in the required ground state to 99.97% , reducing errors and enhancing reliability.

Achievement Metric Significance
MIT fluxonium qubit fidelity 99.998% World record for superconducting single-qubit gates
Quantum refrigerator cooling 22 millikelvin Record-low temperature for autonomous qubit cooling
Molecular quantum entanglement 92% fidelity, ~1 second coherence First sustained entanglement between molecules
Trapped molecule quantum operations 94% accuracy First demonstration of molecules as qubits
Xanadu Aurora system 12 qubits First scalable photonic quantum computer built on server racks
Atom Computing + Microsoft system 50 logical qubits On-premise system supporting error-corrected logical qubits

Investors Vote With Their Wallets: $300M+ in January

Despite stock volatility, private capital flowed aggressively into quantum startups in January.

Startup Funding

  • Alice & Bob raised $104 million in Series B funding (€100M) co-led by Future French Champions, AVP, and Bpifrance. The French startup targets fault-tolerant quantum computers by 2030 using cat qubits that suppress bit-flip errors, requiring thousands rather than millions of physical qubits.

  • SEEQC secured $30 million to develop chip-based quantum systems that integrate classical and quantum processing on the same hardware.

  • Quantum Brilliance raised $20 million to scale production of room-temperature diamond quantum computers, including a mobile quantum computer prototype for a German cybersecurity agency targeting delivery by 2028 .

  • ZuriQ brought in $4.2 million to scale trapped-ion quantum computers with 2D grid architectures.

Government Investment

  • Canada committed over $52 million across 107 quantum projects spanning computing, communications, and sensing. An additional CA$74 million was invested in quantum research commercialization to strengthen global leadership.

  • The U.S. Department of Energy announced a $625 million funding opportunity for National Quantum Information Science Research Centers.

  • Colorado unveiled a $71 million quantum incubator in Boulder to accelerate quantum technology commercialization.

  • Maryland broke ground on a $100 million quantum computing campus at the University of Maryland, featuring a 70,000-square-foot facility for quantum research and development.

Specialized Funds

  • QDNL Participations launched a €25 million fund to support quantum startups globally.

  • Quantonation secured investment from Novo Holdings for its Quantum Venture Fund II , signaling maturation of dedicated quantum VC funds.

New Tools for Quantum Developers

Major product announcements dominated January:

  • Xanadu unveiled Aurora , the first scalable photonic quantum computer built on server racks. The 12-qubit system uses 35 photonic chips and 13 kilometers of fiber optics across four server racks, operating at room temperature. Xanadu envisions scaling to millions of qubits by 2029 using this modular architecture.

  • D-Wave launched the Leap Quantum LaunchPad program, offering a free 3-month trial of its annealing quantum computing technology with support to accelerate application development. More than 100 commercial, government, and research customers have submitted over 200 million problems to D-Wave’s Advantage systems.

  • Atom Computing and Microsoft announced an on-premise quantum system slated for delivery in 2025, featuring over 1,000 physical qubits and supporting up to 50 error-corrected logical qubits . The companies demonstrated 24 logical qubits in 2024 and ran a 28-logical-qubit algorithm.

  • Palo Alto Networks launched a Quantum Random Number Generator (QRNG) Open API framework developed with QRNG innovators including ID Quantique, Qrypt, and Quantinuum. The framework simplifies QRNG integration and aligns with NIST post-quantum cryptography standards, with integration into Next-Generation Firewalls planned for later in 2025.

  • QuEra launched the Quantum Creators Con , a competition running February 3-9 at Columbia University pairing STEM students with creative professionals to produce content about neutral-atom quantum computing.

Quantum Goes Mainstream: Major Partnerships

Traditional institutions are integrating quantum computing:

  • IonQ signed a $21.1 million project with the U.S. Air Force Research Lab to install quantum network infrastructure at the Innovare Advancement Center in New York, advancing secure quantum networking for national security. This builds on a $54.5 million agreement signed in September 2024.

  • Cleveland Clinic and Miami University partnered to establish Ohio’s first specialized degree programs in quantum computing, spanning bachelor’s to doctoral levels. The programs leverage Cleveland Clinic’s IBM Quantum System One—the world’s first quantum computer dedicated to healthcare research—with classes starting in August 2025 .

  • SoftBank Corp. and Quantinuum agreed to launch a joint research initiative integrating quantum computing and AI, aiming to develop solutions that surpass current AI limitations.

  • Telangana (India) partnered with QuantumBasel to establish India’s first Quantum Hub in Hyderabad, focusing on quantum computing and AI applications in finance and life sciences. This aligns with India’s National Quantum Mission, targeting 20-50 qubit quantum computers by 2031 .

  • IonQ renewed its partnership with the UAE’s Technology Innovation Institute to advance quantum research using IonQ Forte systems , expanding access to 36-qubit systems for developing hybrid quantum/classical algorithms.

  • Quantum Computing Inc. collaborated with the Sanders Tri-Institutional Therapeutics Discovery Institute to support computational biomedicine research using Dirac-3 Entropy Quantum Computing machines , which operate at room temperature and low power.

  • The University of Strathclyde partnered with the National Physical Laboratory and Quantum Motion in a three-year project called FIRETRACE to develop tools for measuring thermal behavior of cryogenic electronics—critical for integrating control components with quantum devices.

The Bigger Picture: 2025 as Quantum’s Coming-of-Age

The United Nations proclaimed 2025 the International Year of Quantum Science and Technology , signaling global recognition of the field’s importance. A QuEra Computing report projects a nearly 20% increase in global quantum budgets for 2025, with 65% of quantum professionals feeling prepared for adoption within 2-3 years.

Yet tension persists. After Huang’s comments, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg echoed the skepticism, triggering a second stock drop. The market reaction reflects uncertainty about commercial timelines despite genuine technical progress.

The pattern emerging in January: 2025 isn’t necessarily the year quantum becomes “useful”—it’s the year the field matures from pure research to engineered systems. Google’s Willow chip (announced in December but generating buzz throughout January) demonstrated exponential error reduction and solved a benchmark problem in 5 minutes that would take a supercomputer 10 septillion years .

Investors are diversifying bets across technologies: cat qubits (Alice & Bob), diamond chips (Quantum Brilliance), trapped-ion 2D grids (ZuriQ), photonics (Xanadu), neutral atoms (Atom Computing, QuEra), and superconducting circuits (MIT, Google). No consensus on a winning technology has emerged.

The “Nvidia effect” is a reminder that quantum computing must eventually deliver commercial value, not just scientific breakthroughs. But the technical milestones achieved in January—fidelity records, error correction advances, scalable architectures—represent meaningful progress toward that goal. The field is growing up, even if the path to commercial quantum computing remains longer than some optimists claim.
